episodes.211696: Severe thunderstorm activity occurred across southern portions of Central Alabama from the evening of May 6 into the overnight hours of May 7. Most of the severe weather occurred in the form of wind damage and hail from three distinct supercells across parts of Montgomery, Macon, Greene, Hale, and Sumter counties. Large hail, up to baseball size, was observed just east of downtown Montgomery and later near Forkland in Greene County. As training thunderstorms resulted in 3 to 5 inches of rain falling, several instances of flash flooding occurred in parts of Montgomery, Elmore, Autauga, Marengo, and Sumter counties.
episodes.211993: An outflow boundary from earlier convection resulted in an isolated thunderstorm developing near Peoria during the afternoon of May 7th. Instability was relatively weak, but the storm briefly strengthened and produced one report of nickel-sized hail in Peoria County.
episodes.212035: A storm system with an associated cold front brought widespread showers and thunderstorms to the area, May 6th, lasting into the early overnight hours of May 7th. Several storms became strong to severe with even some localized flash flooding near Columbus, due to the heavy rain.
episodes.213612: Clusters of showers and thunderstorms moved across portions of northwest Florida ahead of a frontal boundary. Several severe weather reports were received with the main impacts to trees and power lines.
episodes.213617: Clusters of showers and thunderstorms moved across portions of southeast Alabama ahead of a frontal boundary. A few severe weather reports were received with the main impacts to trees and power lines.
episodes.213657: A significant severe weather outbreak occurred across northeast Louisiana and central and southern MS amid a favorably sheared environment. A capping inversion limited early convection, which allowed for higher instability. Supercell initiation began in the afternoon and eroded the capping inversion to allow a long track supercell to take root. This supercell produced a long track EF-3 tornados. Several  other brief, weak tornadoes occurred. Supercells also produced hail as large as baseballs and straight line wind damage also occurred. The duration of rainfall also lead to flash flooding.
episodes.213817: A slowly advancing cold front was positioned beneath strong west-southwesterly flow downstream of a broad upper-level trough with embedded shortwaves. A moist low level layer and strong instability combined with strengthening deep-layer and low-level wind shear to support discrete supercells across southwest and southern Mississippi during the late afternoon and evening. These storms produced large hail and multiple tornadoes over southwest Mississippi, one EF1 and one EF2 tornado.
episodes.213964: The 2026 spring breakup along the Yukon River was highly dynamic, defined by a combination of thermal ice decay and severe mechanical ice jams. Because of an exceptionally cold winter and a cool spring, the river ice was thicker than normal and had not deteriorated significantly before the main breakup front arrived. Early-season flooding was driven by localized snowmelt and ice jams on independent river systems and upper sections of the Yukon River.
episodes.214075: A cold front stalled across the region while multiple short waves moved overhead. This produce multiple days of unsettled weather.
episodes.214234: A late Spring storm system brought multiple rounds of thunderstorms to the area on May 6th and 7th. The storms produced wind damage along with large hail a couple of tornadoes.
episodes.214238: A late Spring storm system brought multiple rounds of thunderstorms to the area on May 6th and 7th. The storms produced wind damage along with large hail a couple of tornadoes.
episodes.214239: Thunderstorms moved across the marine area and produced high winds.
episodes.214423: On May 7th, the combination of daytime heating, the sea breeze convergence and the proximity of an upper-level trough produced strong showers and thunderstorms over portions of the Cordillera Central, leading to urban and small stream flooding in Ponce.

Preliminary ground survey confirms EF1 damage beginning along US |Highway 98 between New Augusta and Beaumont, with multiple areas |of softwood and hardwood trees snapped or uprooted. Two |concentrated areas of tree damage were noted along US Highway 98, |suggesting multiple subvortices within a broader circulation. The |maximum intensity occurred around US Highway 98 with winds around |100 mph. The tornado continued generally eastward, crossing |Highway 198 and tracking along or near V L Toussaint Blvd before |weakening over the north side of Beaumont. Farther southwest, |sporadic tree damage was also observed along Highway 29 south of |New Augusta. Satellite data will be examined over the coming weeks|to determine the starting point for the tornado, as radar |suggests that it likely formed over a wooded area southwest of New|Augusta. Further track adjustments are likely once satellite data|is available. ||After review of available Sentinel 2 satellite imagery the |tornado track had major changes to its beginning and end points, |width, and intensity. The tornado was found to have began much |further west to the west of Highway 29 and just north of Red Hill |Road. The tornado traversed forest uprooting and snapping trees |along its path, reaching a peak intensity north of Red Hill Road |where a large section of forest sustained significant damage. Here|wind speeds were likely in the 100 to 110mph range. The tornado |evolved into a multi-vortex evident by several notable corridors |of tree damage along the main tornado track. The tornado continued|east of Highway 29 gradually shrinking in size and weakening. |During this period it dropped southeast a bit along FS Road 312 A.|The tornado began to re- intensify as forest damage became more |noticeable until reaching Highway 98 where ground survey crew |assessed damage. Satellite imagery supported the tornado being |multi-vortex as several focused corridors of damage became evident|as it crossed Highway 98, consistent with ground survey |assessments. Afte the ground survey end point, the tornado did |continue into the forest causing forest damage across Horseshoe |Bend Lake. It then reached the Leaf River where the last evidence |of forest damage associated with the tornado was visible on |Sentinel 2 satellite imagery. This is the estimated end point for |the tornado. The tornado width was also updated to be |approximately 700 yards wide. Additional adjustments are possible |later as high- resolution satellite imagery becomes available over|the next month.

Over the course of two hours and nine minutes, a strong, long|track tornado trekked 81.9 miles across South Mississippi. It|began in southwestern Adams County, then moved across northern|Wilkinson, southeastern Adams, southern Franklin, and central|Lincoln counties, before lifting on the south side of Monticello|in Lawrence County. The tornado intensity peaked at a high-end EF3|with an estimated maximum wind of 160 MPH just east of Garden|City in southwestern Franklin County. The maximum path width was|1.5 miles in east central Lincoln County.||The tornado began in the St. Catherine Creek National Wildlife|Refuge in southwestern Adams County, causing sporadic tree damage|as it crossed US Hwy 61, Will Washington Rd, and the Homochitto|River into northern Wilkinson County. The path straddled the|Wilkinson and Adams County line for 7-8 miles, remaining mainly on|the Wilkinson County side, but producing damage on the Adams County|side at times as it strengthened. The tornado then fully re-|entered the southeasternmost corner of Adams County, producing|heavy timber damage over a 3/4 to 1 mile wide footprint as it|entered the Homochitto National Forest for the first time. Here, a|few swaths of tree damage began to reach EF2 thresholds.||Crossing into southwestern Franklin County, heavy timber damage,|reaching EF2 intensity at times, continued into the Garden City|community. A few structures were impacted in this area, including|multiple buildings with roof damage, a mobile home that was|destroyed, and multiple outbuildings that were destroyed. The|tornado reached its peak intensity as it continued east-|northeastward and reentered the Homochitto National Forest. As it|crossed Freewood Road, it intensified, snapping a high percentage|of trees through dense pine forest and mixed forest tracts. While|tree damage was extensive in this area, ground surveys revealed|there were numerous dead snags throughout this section of the|forest, possibly impacted by prior drought, fire, or some|combination thereof. As a result, it was determined that several|of the trees along the damage path originally believed to be|debarked by the tornado were already without bark or had bark that|was easily stripped. Still, extensive damage to the healthy trees|through this portion of southwestern Franklin County warranted a|high end EF3 rating. The tornado remained strong as it crossed|Bunkley Road twice, then weakened slightly as it crossed the|Homochitto River. It continued producing periodic EF2 damage east|of Gloster Road and as it crossed US Highway 98 near Okhissa Lake,|where the nearby Bude RAWS site recorded a 76 mph gust on the|south side of the track. East of the lake, the tornado weakened|further to EF0-EF1 intensity, leaving patches of downed trees|across Berrytown, Bogue Chitto, Burt Jordan, Murray, and Olympia|Roads before moving into western Lincoln County.||The tornado began to intensify again as it passed near the West|Lincoln community, producing EF2 damage as it crossed West Lincoln|Drive and briefly reaching EF3 intensity just east of that|location, bodily removing two trees and moving them 5 to 10 yards.|There was also a large portion of a snapped pine was thrown about|30 to 40 yards into a field in the same location. As the tornado|approached Jackson Liberty Road, the tornado collapsed a lattice|electrical transmission tower and removed the top half of another.|Along Auburn Drive, multiple mobile homes were destroyed, two|houses sustained major roof loss, and two vehicles were moved. The|tornado then crossed Calvary Drive, Apple Trail, and Pecan Lane,|causing widespread timber loss and further structural roof damage.|After crossing I-55, the storm reached low-end EF3 strength near|Stoneybrook Trail, where a home suffered exterior wall failure and|extensive tree damage and some tree debarking was observed.|Crossing US Highway 51, the tornado swept directly through a|mobile home park, destroying 10 to 20 mobile homes and tossing|several vehicles. Additional mobile homes were destroyed just east|of Highway 51 north of Hog Chain Drive, with severe tree damage|persisting near the Bogue Chitto River.||Pushing into eastern Lincoln County, the circulation widened|significantly expanding up to 1.5 miles wide east of Pricedale|Drive. Widespread EF2 damage continued across Pricedale Drive and|Mount Olive Road, with the tornado destroying a mobile home,|heavily damaging several houses, and impacting multiple farm|buildings. At a destroyed hay shed, a single hay bale was moved 10|to 20 yards toward the center of the path. Near the Enterprise|community, tree damage spiked once more, and several homes|suffered major roof damage across MS Highway 583, Mallalieu Drive,|and surrounding roads. After crossing East Lincoln Road near|Wellman Drive, the tornado tracked east-northeastward toward|Harmony. Along Harmony Drive, it destroyed multiple chicken houses|and damaged several homes. Severe timber damage including partial|debarking continued east of Pleasant Grove Drive as the tornado|approached the Lawrence County line.||The tornado maintained EF2 intensity into western Lawrence|County, with significant damage to timber continuing across Trace|Road and Ford Calcote Road. In this area, a barn and mobile home|were demolished. Another home sustained heavy roof damage as the|tornado paralleled Lower Brookhaven Road. It then began to weaken|as it crossed Carmel Road and Carmel New Hope Road, then lifted on|the south side of Monticello, just east of MS Highway 27 near|Halls Creek.
Flash flooding occurred around the Millbrook and Coosada areas, with a video received of flooding at Pineleaf Dr and Dogwood Cir.

After review of available medium to high resolution satellite|imagery, it was determined an EF1 tornado occurred near Jonathan.|This tornado began southwest of Highway 63 where it began causing|intermittent tree damage across portions of the forest. After|crossing Highway 63, it moved into some open fields where it|continued to cause tree damage in a focused corridor. The tornado|strengthened on approach to Jonathan Road where a more persistent|corridor of tree damage was able to be observed. The tornado|continued northeast across Jonathan Road, reaching its peak|intensity around 90mph just northwest of Albert Smith Road where|a corridor of more substantial treefall was evident on satellite|imagery. The damage path becomes intermittent after this point,|with the last visible tree damage east of the Albert Smith Road|and Old Avera Road intersection. This is also where the radar|tornado debris signature dissipates, and no further damage is|evident further east via satellite imagery. Adjustments to the|tornado are possible later as high-resolution satellite imagery|becomes available over the next month.

An EF-0 tornado began on the south side of Prentiss near MS Highway 13 and tracked across Old Highway 13, Tom Bullock Road, and MS Highway 42. A storm chaser observed turbulent debris and power flashes. As it approached the Lake Jeff Davis area, it began to occlude and tracked along Ed Parkman Road and then lifted. Along this path, several small trees and various tree limbs were downed. The estimated maximum wind speeds were 80 mph.
Reports of street flooding along U.S. Highway 80 in Demopolis.

Numerous instances of flooding around Prattville following 4 to 5 inches of rain. Reports of flooding included Golson Road and U.S. Highway 82 Bypass, Briarwood St, near Summer Hill Rd and Doster Rd, Sheila Blvd and Tara Dr, Sydney Dr and Kendrick Way, North Chestnut St and West 5th St, Cooters Pond Rd, and the entrance to White Oak Ct.

This tornado began near Oilwell Road and tracked across Wilson Road near Burkhalter Road, lifting shortly thereafter. Along the path, several large hardwoods were uprooted and part of the roof was blown off of a shed. The estimated maximum wind speed was 95 mph.
A concentrated area of tree and power line damage occurred along Salem Church Road.
Part of Sumter County Road 22 was washed out near Belmont following heavy rainfall totals of 3 to 4 inches across the area.

A 10-mile-long ice jam formed several river bends below Chalkyitsik on the Draanjik River. It completely blocked the channel, pushing large chunks of ice onshore and causing river levels in the community to rise slowly but continuously for several days. Public and emergency mangers reported flooding in Chalkyiksik, with low-lying and poor drainage areas experiencing most of the flooding. By Saturday May 9th, the ice jam had broken up downriver and conditions had improved.
Barn destroyed near intersection of Slaughter Road and GA Hwy 41.
A portion of J E Johnson Avenue was washed out within Prentiss city limits.
Flash flooding led to water rescues of six people on Lucas Warner Road and Highway 84 West.
Four homes were flooded. One home was located near Highway 84 E on Cedar Grove Road.
A home was flooded on Ponderosa Road.
A large section of Rowan Road was under water and parts were washed out.
Trees were blown down near Ruth.
Trees were blown down along Holmesville Road.

A NWS ground survey confirmed an EF-1 tornado with maximum sustained winds of 95 mph tracked across portions of northern Walthall County, near Enon, MS. This tornado began near L. L. Coon Rd where high resolution satellite imagery showed areas of damaged/displaced trees on a confined path that tracked southeast toward MS Hwy 44. The tornado strengthened to EF-1 strength as it moved into Willie Cothern Rd where it uprooted trees, lifted metal roofing off a porch, and snapped a swath of tree trunks on private property. The tornado turned more eastward as it crossed MS Hwy 583 where it damaged shingles on a church and uprooted and snapped a few trees. Minor tree damage continued eastward across New Home Church Road with plenty of tree debris across the road. The tornado then restrengthened some over inaccessible forested areas south of New Home Church Rd where patches of heavier tree damage/displacement was identified on high resolution satellite imagery. This tree damage gradually became more minor again near Hope Rd and Dee Toney Rd. Numerous small trees were leaning in a confluent pattern with large branches down near MS Hwy 27. Minor tree damage continued with uproots and large branches predominantly occurring along the damage path on Jordan, Sauls, and Dan Holmes roads. This tornado continued east-southeast into Marion County, within the NWS Jackson area of responsibility, where additional EF-0 and EF-1 tree damage was identified by ground survey. It's estimated that the tornado finally lifted near Circle Bar Road after being on the ground for approximately 13 miles and 24 minutes.
A culvert was washed out on Mt. Williams Road.
A vehicle was swept off the road on Ora Street. Emergency personnel rescued the occupant from the vehicle.
Southbound lanes of Highway 49 were flooded.
Flash flooding led to minor street flooding in the Laurel area.

A NWS ground survey confirmed an EF-1 tornado with maximum sustained winds of 95 mph tracked across portions of northern Walthall County, near Enon, MS. This tornado began near L. L. Coon Rd where high resolution satellite imagery showed areas of damaged and displaced trees on a confined path that tracked southeast toward MS Highway 44. The tornado strengthened to EF-1 strength as it moved into Willie Cothern Road where it uprooted trees, lifted metal roofing off a porch, and snapped a swath of tree trunks on private property. The tornado turned more eastward as it crossed MS Highway 583 where it damaged shingles on a church and uprooted and snapped a few trees. Minor tree damage continued eastward across New Home Church Road with plenty of tree debris across the road. The tornado then restrengthened some over inaccessible forested areas south of New Home Church Road where patches of heavier tree damage and displacement was identified on high resolution satellite imagery. This tree damage gradually became more minor again near Hope Road and Dee Toney Road. Numerous small trees were leaning in a confluent pattern with large branches down near MS Highway 27. Minor tree damage continued with uproots and large branches predominantly occurring along the damage path on Jordan, Sauls, and Dan Holmes roads. This tornado continued east-southeast into Marion County, within the NWS Jackson MS area of responsibility near the community of Darbun, where additional EF-0 and EF-1 tree damage was identified by ground survey. It's estimated that the tornado finally lifted near Circle Bar Road after being on the ground for approximately 16.5 miles and 24 minutes.
Tree fell onto structure along 3700 Block of Briar Drive in Lithia Springs. No injuries reported.

Preliminary ground survey confirms low end EF1 damage northeast|of Grand Bay, Alabama. Maximum intensity of 88 mph was found on|Jim McNeil Loop Road where several large tree limbs were down|over a compact area. The tornado tracked southeast and produced|sporadic damage on Dedicated Road where a horse trailer was|flipped and more trees were damaged. After passing over Old|Pascagoula Road, additional tree damage with downed limbs and|snapped trees were found on Wells Road West. Satellite data will|be examined in the coming weeks to confirm the starting point of|the tornado, which is likely further to the northwest in wooded|areas over Jackson Creek east of Grand Bay Wilmer Road.||After review of available Sentinel 2 satellite imagery, the |beginning and end points of the tornado have been adjusted to |reflect a narrow corridor of persistent tree damage along the |tornado track. The start point is brought back to just south of |Davis Lane along Jackson Creek where minor tree damage becomes |evident. The end point was adjusted southeast across Interstate 10|where tree damage became apparent again in the vicinity of Boe |Road and Henley Road, in line with the location that the radar TDS|began to dissipate. No additional damage is visible southeast of |this location. Further refinements of the track are possible later|as higher resolution imagery becomes available.
A tree was down on Highway 77 near Graceville.
A tree was down on Mill Creek Road.
A tree was down on Highway 79 near Bonifay.

Available Sentinel 2 satellite imagery and available radar data|with a tornado debris signature revealed a weak EF0 tornado|occurred near Theodore Industrial Park. Minor tree damage was|evident, beginning along the tree line north of Degussa Road.|This is where the first signs of a radar tornado debris signature|appear. The tornado crossed Rangeline Road, producing another|small corridor of tree damage west of Dauphin Island Parkway|along Cedar Wood Drive North. The damage path comes to an end at|Dauphin Island Parkway and serves as the end point for this|tornado.

Trees were down on power lines on Highway 79 North of Vernon.
